hookVariants.narration: Sixty thousand euros into a shared house, and on paper it can look like a gift.

beats.narration: Under a joint tenancy, each death passes that share to the remaining owners. In a group, the last survivor may own everything.
beats.subtext: The last survivor gets the house

beats.narration: Mira and Tobias are married, and the title names them. Kai, their partner, put in sixty thousand euros. When Mira dies, Tobias owns everything.
The other common form holds the home in stated shares. Shares can match what each person put in. Fifty, thirty and twenty percent, say.
beats.subtext: Shares match what each put in

beats.narration: Each share then passes under its owner's will. Without one, it goes to that owner's relatives, who then share the house with the group.
beats.subtext: So each owner needs a will

beats.narration: Three records would have helped Kai: stated shares on the title, a written record of the sixty thousand, and a will for each owner.
A common surprise: under a joint tenancy, a will cannot pass the share on. The other owners take it first.
Property rules vary by country. Three questions matter: who owns each share, where it goes after a death, and what happens when someone leaves.

caption.instagram:
Three partners paid for a house. One died. The partner who put in €60,000 owned nothing.

Mira and Tobias are married, and Kai has been their partner for six years. The title names the couple as joint tenants. Kai put in €60,000 of the deposit and a third of every payment, with nothing in writing. Under a joint tenancy, a death passes the share to the other owners, so when Mira dies, Tobias owns the whole house. Held in stated shares instead, each share passes under its owner's will, which means each owner needs one. The names and the rules differ by country, and forced heirship limits a will in some.

Three questions for any shared title: who owns what fraction, where does a share go on a death, and what happens if someone wants out?
